title: Synergistic remineralisation of enamel adjacent to orthodontic brackets using self-assembling peptide with calcium phosphate and fluoride systems: An in vitro study.
byline: Simmuni S, Mandava P, K PP, et al.
html:
Objective: To compare the remineralisation potential of self-assembling peptide P11-4 (SAP), casein phosphopeptide-amorphous calcium phosphate (CPP-ACP), fluoride-enriched CPP-ACP (CPP-ACFP) and their combinations under a dynamic pH-cycling model simulating conditions adjacent to orthodontic brackets.

Methods: This in vitro study included 104 sound human premolars that were demineralised and randomly allocated to eight groups (n = 13): control, SAP, fluoride varnish (F), CPP-ACP, CPP-ACFP, SAP + F, SAP + CPP-ACP and SAP + CPP-ACFP. Specimens underwent 28 demineralisation-remineralisation cycles over 30 days. Quantitative light-induced fluorescence assessed fluorescence loss (ΔF, %) and integrated fluorescence loss (ΔQ, mm² × %) at four intervals (T 1 -T 4 ). Intra- and inter-group differences were analysed using Friedman, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis and Bonferroni-adjusted Mann-Whitney tests (α = 0.05).

Results: All experimental groups showed significant time-dependent remineralisation ( P < 0.001). SAP + CPP-ACFP showed the greatest cumulative improvement (ΔF ΔT = +6.27; ΔQ ΔT = +4.4), followed by SAP + CPP-ACP and SAP + F. Among the individual agents, CPP-ACFP showed greater improvement than CPP-ACP, fluoride varnish and SAP. Combination regimens produced 20%-30% greater improvement than the individual agents.

Conclusions: All regimens produced measurable remineralisation, with SAP + CPP-ACFP showing the most favourable response. The findings support the complementary action of peptide-guided crystal nucleation and fluoride-stabilised calcium-phosphate replenishment and suggest a promising minimally invasive approach for managing orthodontically induced white-spot lesions.

How a tooth-repair gel combined with calcium, phosphate and fluoride may repair early enamel damage around fixed braces Why was the study done? White spots can develop around fixed braces when acids remove minerals from tooth enamel. Fluoride and calcium-phosphate products help replace these minerals, mainly near the enamel surface. A new tooth-repair self-assembling peptide gel forms a network and support within damaged enamel that may support new mineral growth. This study tested to know if this gel would work better when used with fluoride, calcium and phosphate products. What did the researchers do? The laboratory study used extracted human premolar teeth mimicking the white spot–like lesions seen in people with braces. The teeth were divided into groups and the healing capacity tested in different combinations with and without new gel. The teeth went through repeated acid and repair cycles to copy daily mouth conditions. A special light was used to measure how much mineral was lost and how much was restored over time. What did the researchers find? All treatments helped repair early tooth decay. The best results were seen when the new gel was combined with fluoride and calcium-phosphate. This improved repair by about 20%—30% compared to single products. The repair was stronger and reached deeper into the tooth. What do the findings mean? Early tooth decay during fixed braces can be treated better using a combination approach. For patients, this means a gentle and pain-free method to heal early decay and prevent further damage to the tooth.
